# Subject kind recipe (v1)

Schema for `.tera/subject-kinds/<name>.hcl` recipes per [ADR-100](../adr/ADR-100-subjects-and-observations.md) D1. A **subject** is `<kind>/<id>` — `device/porch-temp`, `machine/4`, `test/TestShimServerSpawnsWithCredential`. This recipe declares the **kind** half, and it is the whole of what a deployment declares: the `<id>` half is free text, opaque to tera, and is whatever the domain already calls the thing. An undeclared kind is refused; a validated *id* would oblige every deployment to mirror an inventory tera has no business owning. The file stem is the kind name, so `device.hcl` declares `device/…`. The recipe declares a single `subject_kind` block whose label must equal that stem.

| Regime | persisted |
| Identity regime | `recipe` — the filename stem is the identity; the file declares exactly one resource, and a block label — where the grammar admits one — must equal the stem (ADR-087 D3) |
| Current version | `v1` |
| Supported versions | `v1` |
| Schema `$id` | `https://kottera.dev/schemas/recipe/subject-kind/v1` |
| Go source | `github.com/kottera/kottera/pkg/systemvault/schemas.subjectKindRecipe` |
| Served at | `GET /api/v1/schemas/recipe/subject-kind/{version}` |

## Example

A minimal `subject-kind`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/subject-kinds/example-subject-kind.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

subject_kind "example-subject-kind" {
  mode = "instance"
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | string | yes | — | — | const `v1` | Per-recipe grammar version. Required; this schema applies when version is v1. |
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | min length 1 | Bare subject-kind name (the HCL block label), which must equal the filename stem. It is the kind half of every subject key of this kind: a recipe named device declares the device in device/porch-temp. The loader namespaces the recipe as <vault-id>/subject-kinds/<name>. RESERVED: workorder, work_order, work-order and wo are refused at load, compared case-insensitively. ADR-100 D1 rules that a Work Order is never a subject under any kind, because the ADR-096 about relation already means this work is examining that Work Order - so a workorder/<uuid7> kind would be a second spelling of a shipped referent, and a reader asking what work is about a Work Order would find half the answer in each record. To say that a Work Order is about another Work Order, name the operand with about_input on the work_order_type instead; this recipe declares kinds of things in the world, which a Work Order is not. |
| `mode` | string | yes | — | — | one of `instance`, `role` | Continuity mode (ADR-100 D2): what happens to the observations about a subject of this kind when the thing that subject denotes is REPLACED. instance - the subject denotes a particular physical or logical article, so replacement bumps an epoch and observations from prior epochs are retired rather than carried forward (a swapped sensor makes a confident wrong answer, which is worse than no answer). role - the subject denotes a position that outlives its occupant, so observations survive replacement (a rebuilt spindle does not reset what the station is for). Required, and there is deliberately NO DEFAULT: the two are indistinguishable from a kind spelling - one deployment keys device/<serial> as instance and device/<install-site> as role - so a default would be a safety-relevant choice made by absence, and a subject_kind declaring no mode fails to load. STILL INERT, AND NO LONGER FOR ITS ORIGINAL REASON: observations have been recorded since Wave 2 of PLAN-2026-08-learned-operational-knowledge and each one carries the epoch this field is about, but NOTHING BUMPS ONE - there is no epoch counter, and the replacement operation that would move it is unbuilt - so today this field is declared, validated and stored, and governs no behaviour you can observe. It is mandatory now rather than later because adding a mandatory no-default field to a kind that already has recipes in the wild invalidates every one of them at load, which is a breakage rather than a migration. |
| `body_schema` | string | no | — | — | — | Raw JSON Schema for the TYPED HALF of an observation about this kind, written as an HCL heredoc (ADR-100 D4). It is the whole of what a kind declares about the record: the contract owns subjects, summary, confidence, provenance, the timestamps, supersedes and epoch, and the kind owns this and nothing else. Validated as a JSON Schema at load, so a malformed one fails while you are reading the file that holds it rather than at the first observation that happens to carry a body; there is no fall back to accepting everything when it will not compile. OMITTING IT IS A PROHIBITION, NOT A PERMISSION: a kind that declares no body_schema REFUSES an observation carrying a body, because the schema is the prescription and a body nothing prescribes records a shape no consumer can read. No permissive stand-in is inferred. Writing body_schema = "" is refused rather than read as absence, for the same reason - the way to say this kind prescribes no body is to omit the attribute, and an author who writes it blank would otherwise inherit that prohibition without asking for it. IT MUST BE SELF-CONTAINED: an internal reference (#/$defs/...) is fine, and any $ref the compiler would have to fetch or read off the daemon's disk is refused, because the recipe is the declaration and a schema whose meaning lives in a second file is one no vault carries and no review sees. The precedent is payload_schema on a work_order_type checkpoints block, copied including that posture. |
| `decay_after` | string | no | `1440h` | — | — | Staleness clock (ADR-100 D8): how long an observation about a subject of this kind stands before it is stale. A Go duration string, so 1440h is 60 days and 720h is 30. The default of 1440h is MEASURED rather than chosen - it is the re-verification window enforced by tests/codestyle/flake_registry_test.go, the one hand-built observation store this repository already runs, and D8 generalizes that store's mechanism rather than guessing a fresh number. ON EXPIRY AN OBSERVATION IS NOT DELETED: it drops to suspected and is flagged for re-verification, because deletion loses the provenance the D7 blast-radius query needs, and that query is asked most urgently about a claim that has just turned out to be wrong. Must be positive, and there is no spelling for never: 0 and an empty value are both refused rather than read as an opt-out D8 does not ratify. It carries a default while mode does not, and D8 states the rule that separates them - NO-DEFAULT IS RESERVED FOR CHOICES WHERE ABSENCE IS DANGEROUS, so a continuity mode guessed wrong delivers a confident falsehood while a staleness clock guessed long costs an observation more standing than it earned, which re-verification corrects. Making every knob mandatory would spend the authoring budget that makes the two dangerous ones conspicuous. LIVE, and read by a sweep this deployment has to INSTALL: D8 ratifies curation as a scheduled worker shipped as a documented example rather than a seed default, so the capability that enforces this clock (observations.decay) ships in the daemon and nothing runs it until a deployment installs a trigger - examples/observation-curator/ is that example. A deployment that has not installed one has a declared clock nothing enforces, which is the ratified default and not a defect. Withdrawing the kind does not stop the clock: the value is frozen at its last declared reading and its observations go on decaying on it (D10 Amendment 3 part 1). |
| `identity_key` | string[] | no | — | — | — | CLAIM IDENTITY (ADR-100 D10 Amendment 1): which body_schema properties make two observations THE SAME CLAIM. Two observations sharing a subject set, an epoch and the values of every property named here are one claim, and a second author making the same claim CORROBORATES it - which is what promotes an observation and widens it past the domain that wrote it. Nothing infers identity from similarity: the key is deployment-declared and matched exactly, on the decoded and canonicalized JSON value rather than on raw bytes, so 4 and 4.0 and a whitespace difference never decide a visibility question. EVERY NAMED PROPERTY MUST BE DECLARED AND REQUIRED BY body_schema, checked at load, and the refusal says which of the two it failed. The required half is the load-bearing one: an OPTIONAL identity property means two observations that both omit it match on absent-equals-absent, and corroboration would then widen visibility on the emptiest possible evidence - a null must never be the reason something became readable across a domain. The check reads body_schema's own top-level properties and required and does not descend into allOf, $ref or conditional composition, so a composed schema has to restate the identity properties at top level; it can refuse a schema whose property really is required a level down, and it can never admit one it has not seen required. THE PROSE SUMMARY IS NEVER PART OF IDENTITY - it is contract rather than body, so it is not nameable here, and it is called out because it is the field an author reaches for first. TOP-LEVEL PROPERTY NAMES ONLY: there is no path grammar, because a path means owning JSON Pointer escaping, array indexing and what a path through a missing object means, on a compare that decides an authorization outcome - hoist the field instead, since a path syntax is additive later and could never be taken back. OMITTING THE ATTRIBUTE IS WARNED ABOUT, NOT REFUSED: observations of a kind with no identity key can never be corroborated and will never leave the domain that wrote them, which is the safe direction from one side and a dead letter from the other. Writing identity_key = [] means exactly the same thing and is accepted in silence, so an author who has considered the question has a way to say so. |
| `promotion_threshold` | integer | no | `2` | — | minimum 1 | Evidence bar (ADR-100 D8): how many INDEPENDENT corroborations promote an observation about a subject of this kind. Defaults to 2; must be at least 1, because a threshold below one promotes an observation nothing corroborated, which is a writer asserting verified about its own claim by another route. Independent is D4's author_class rule applied - one run's three retries are one witness, not three - so this counts corroborating authors rather than records. It is per kind rather than per deployment because the bar differs sharply WITHIN one deployment: a test/ flake earns promotion on a second corroboration, while a machine/ safety claim should want more of them and from different author classes, so a deployment-wide number is wrong for both ends at once. Promotion is a curator action and never a property of the writer: a run that observes something writes suspected, and no writer may assert verified about its own observation (D5). It carries a default while mode does not, for D8's stated reason - no-default is reserved for choices where absence is dangerous, and a promotion threshold guessed low costs an observation more credence than it earned, which the curator's contradiction pass and D5's supersession both correct. NOT INERT: the corroboration-widening promoter reads it in this same wave. |
| `delivery_record` | boolean | no | `false` | — | — | Whether a resolution — pull or push — that delivered an observation about a subject of this kind writes a durable delivery record of having done so (ADR-100 D7). OPT-IN PER KIND, DEFAULTING OFF: the dev queue declares neither this nor delivery_retention and pays nothing, a regulated line turns it on for machine/ and batch/, and a building-automation deployment turns it on with SHORT retention for occupant-privacy kinds. Two questions are answered by this record and by nothing else in the system. What did the agent know when it made this decision — the regulated-batch audit question, asked years later, which cannot be answered from telemetry-with-prompts because sampling is set for performance by people not thinking about audit, stream retention is not archival retention, not every consumer has a prompt at all, and retaining years of full prompts to satisfy an observation audit is a liability rather than an asset. And: this observation was just refuted, what did it contaminate — the blast-radius query, which runs backwards from the observation to the dispatches that consumed it, and which is the justification that stands alone, because an observation store with no recall path can poison work it cannot identify. The record is small, structured and unsampled — a durable INDEX INTO telemetry rather than a second copy of it — and it carries a trace_id so the full-fidelity rendering is one hop away for as long as the trace survives. LIVE SINCE WAVE 3 ITEM 7 of PLAN-2026-08-learned-operational-knowledge: a resolution touching a subject of a kind that declares this writes the record, from ONE writer reached by both delivery directions. What is recorded per observation is its id and THE STANDING IT WAS DELIVERED WITH — confidence and last_verified — because there is no version and confidence is mutated in place, so an id-only record would answer the headline question wrongly rather than partially (D7 Amendment 1). Per delivery it records the mode that actually rendered and whether that mode was DEGRADED under D6's bound, plus the consuming dispatch's own trust domain, its work_order_id where there was one, the matched subjects and the trace_id. A resolution touching NO kind that declares this writes nothing at all — not an empty record — and a resolution spanning declaring and non-declaring kinds records only the declaring half, because the opt-in is a property of the kind and a record naming a subject of a kind that declined the audit trail would be exactly that trail. |
| `delivery_retention` | string | no | — | — | — | How long a delivery record about a subject of this kind is kept, as a Go duration string. REQUIRED WHEN delivery_record = true, AND THERE IS DELIBERATELY NO DEFAULT — the one place in this grammar where ADR-100 D8's no-default rule bites the other way. D7's own examples are a regulated line keeping the record for years and a building-automation deployment keeping it briefly for occupant-privacy kinds, so a default would make the privacy case silently long, which is exactly the class no-default is reserved for: a choice whose absence is dangerous. Setting it while delivery_record is false or absent is REFUSED rather than ignored, in the posture a checkpoints payload_schema already takes when phases is empty — an author who wrote a retention believes something about how long a record is kept, and there is no record. Must parse as a Go duration and be positive: a record retained for no time is a record that was never written, and the way to say that is delivery_record = false. A prior delivery record is IMMUTABLE and keeps the subject id it was written with (ADR-100 D2) — rewriting it to match a later name is precisely what an audit trail exists to prevent. ENFORCED SINCE WAVE 3 ITEM 7: a daemon-side sweep deletes records past their retention, and deletion here IS deletion, unlike D8's decay, which costs an observation its standing and never its row — the whole reason for a short retention is the occupant-privacy case, where retaining the row is the liability. A record can name several kinds and THE SHORTEST RETENTION AMONG THEM GOVERNS: a retention is a ceiling on how long a record may be kept, so the tightest ceiling on a record wins, and the alternative reading would silently extend a short retention for exactly the resolutions that touched two things. A record naming a kind the deployment has since WITHDRAWN IS STILL SWEPT: D10 Amendment 3 part 1 FREEZES every clock a subject_kind declares at its last declared value rather than stopping it, so the sweep goes on running against the retention the withdrawn kind last declared. Amendment 2 had been implemented as stopping that clock, which held such a record forever — right for an audit trail and exactly backwards for the occupant-privacy kind short retentions exist for. A live declaration always wins, so a retention an operator SHORTENS takes effect on the very next pass and the value is pinned only once nothing can edit it. WITHDRAWAL IS NOT DELETION: an operator who means stop holding this rather than stop using this purges explicitly (Amendment 3 part 2 — tera observations purge --kind <kind>, its own grant, its own audit event, not reversible), and tera config plan WARNS when the transition would withdraw a kind that still holds records, naming the count and both dispositions, so the choice is made where it is visible rather than discovered a quarter later (Amendment 3 part 3). Deletion happens between the declared retention and that retention plus one sweep interval. |
